review_flags: Book wording: the text says the "[\w]+" regex "will grab consecutive non-whitespace characters". Strictly, \w matches word characters (letters, digits, underscore); non-whitespace would be \S. For example, "isn't" splits into "isn" and "t" with the apostrophe dropped, because "'" is neither \w nor in [.,!?;]. The notes explain the actual behaviour.
Minor: the printed REPL outputs use double quotes (["T", "h", ...]), while a real Python REPL prints lists of strings with single quotes. The content is the same.

overview.title: Word splitting with regex, indexing, and the idea of a vocabulary
overview.main_topic: Character and word splitting with regular expressions, then mapping tokens to integer indices through a vocabulary instead of raw ASCII codes
overview.central_idea: After splitting text into tokens (characters or words-plus-punctuation), we index them: each token is mapped to a unique integer. ASCII/Unicode code points scale poorly, so NLP builds a vocabulary, a mapping from the tokens that actually occur in the training data to indices, which works equally well for characters and words.
overview.importance: Indexing via a vocabulary is the standard bridge from strings to the integer tensors that every text model in the book consumes, from bag-of-words models to embeddings and Transformers.

Understand the alternation regex [\w]+|[.,!?;] and what split_words returns

Explain why ASCII/Unicode codes scale poorly and why a vocabulary is more robust
Begin to read the dictionary-based vocabulary that continues on p.410

summary:
The page continues the hands-on introduction to text preprocessing. First it shows the result of the character splitter from p.408: `split_chars("The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.")[:12]` gives `["T", "h", "e", " ", "q", "u", "i", "c", "k", " ", "b", "r"]`. Every character, spaces included, is a token.

Next the authors switch to **word-level splitting** by combining two patterns with the regex alternation `|`: `[\w]+` grabs a run of word characters, and `[.,!?;]` matches a single punctuation mark from that set. `split_words` returns `re.findall(r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]", text)`; on the test sentence "The quick brown fox jumped over the dog." it yields `["The", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumped", "over", "the", "dog", "."]`. The final period is a separate token, and the capital "T" is kept.

Splitting produces string tokens, but models need numbers. The most common approach is **indexing**: map each token to a unique integer. The authors call this flexible and reversible, and note that how indices are later mapped into a latent space the model ingests (for example, embeddings) is a separate decision.

For characters one could index with ASCII codes, `ord('A')` -> 65 and `ord('z')` -> 122, but this scales poorly across languages, since Unicode defines over a million characters. The more robust technique is a **vocabulary**: a mapping built from the tokens that actually occur in our training data to indices. It works for word tokens as easily as for character tokens. The page ends by starting to build such a vocabulary as a Python dictionary, `"[UNK]": 0, "the": 1, "quick": 2, "brown": 3, "fox": 4, "jumped": 5, ...`, which continues on p.410.

paragraphs.excerpt: Regex can easily be applied to split our text into words instead.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors move from character to word splitting. The pattern "[\w]+" grabs consecutive characters (the book says "non-whitespace characters"), and "[.,!?;]" matches one of the listed punctuation marks. Combining the two gives a regex that turns each word and each punctuation mark into a token.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The combined pattern [\w]+|[.,!?;] reads: "a run of one or more word characters, OR a single punctuation mark from this set." re.findall applies it left to right, so words come out whole, punctuation comes out as its own token, and spaces (which match neither branch) are skipped.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is a simple word-level tokenizer, the second of the two approaches proposed on p.408. Treating punctuation as separate tokens means "dog." and "dog" share the token "dog".
paragraphs.technical_idea: Precisely, \w matches word characters (Unicode letters, digits and underscore), not all non-whitespace; \S is the non-whitespace class. Characters such as apostrophes, hyphens or quotes are dropped by this regex, so "isn't" becomes ["isn", "t"]. The brackets in [\w]+ are redundant (\w+ is equivalent).

terminology.meaning: Regex class for word characters: letters, digits and underscore (Unicode-aware in Python 3).
Matches any single character listed inside the brackets, e.g. [.,!?;].
Matches either the pattern on its left or the one on its right.
Quantifier: one or more repetitions of the preceding item.

paragraphs.excerpt: Splitting takes us from a single string to a token sequence, but
paragraphs.what_it_says: Splitting gives a sequence of string tokens, but we still need numbers. By far the most common approach is to map each token to a unique integer index, called indexing the input. It is a flexible and reversible representation that works with many modelling approaches; how indices are later mapped into a latent space ingested by the model can be decided later.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Indexing separates two concerns. The first is identity: which token is this? An integer answers it. The second is representation: what vector does the model use for it? That can be decided later as one-hot, multi-hot or learned embeddings. Because the mapping is one-to-one (on known tokens), you can go back from indices to tokens.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The integer sequence is the common currency of NLP pipelines. Keras' TextVectorization layer, embedding layers and the Transformer all consume token indices, and chapter 15 reverses the mapping to generate text (p.446).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Reversible only for tokens in the vocabulary: once unknown tokens collapse to [UNK] (p.410), the original string cannot be recovered. Standardization (p.410) is also lossy.

terminology.meaning: Mapping each token to a unique integer.
The learned vector space into which the model maps token indices, e.g. via an embedding layer.

connections: p.446: detokenizing maps integers back to string tokens for text generation.
p.433: word embeddings are one way to map indices into a latent space.

paragraphs.excerpt: For character tokens, we could use ASCII lookups to index each token—for
paragraphs.what_it_says: For characters, ASCII lookups could serve as indices, e.g. ord('A') -> 65 and ord('z') -> 122. But this scales poorly to other languages, since the Unicode specification has over a million characters. A more robust technique is to build a mapping from the tokens in our training data to indices, which NLP calls a vocabulary. It works for word-level tokens as easily as for character-level ones.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Using a fixed global code (ASCII/Unicode code points) as the index means the index space is as big as the whole character set, mostly filled with characters you will never see, which is wasteful when indices feed one-hot vectors or embedding tables. A vocabulary uses only the tokens that occur in the data you care about, so the index range stays compact. And words have no global numbering at all, so a vocabulary is the only option for them.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Vocabulary size becomes a key hyperparameter in the following sections (e.g. limiting to the most frequent tokens), and it directly sets the size of embedding matrices and output softmax layers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Python's ord returns a Unicode code point (0 to 1,114,111); ASCII is the subset 0-127. An embedding table indexed by raw code points would need over a million rows.

terminology.meaning: Python built-in returning the integer Unicode code point of a single character.
The universal character standard, with a code space of over a million positions.
A mapping from the tokens found in the training data to integer indices.

connections: p.408: ASCII-style character indexing was first suggested there.
p.411: Keras tokenization layers build vocabularies automatically from data.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors announce a small demo: build a Python dictionary mapping tokens to indices, split the input into tokens and index them. The dictionary begins with "[UNK]": 0 and then lists the words of the example sentence with increasing indices.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A vocabulary is just a lookup table. Index 0 is reserved for a special unknown token, and the remaining entries are lowercase words in order of first appearance ("the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumped", ...). The listing continues overleaf with "over", "dog" and "."; "lazy" is deliberately left out.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This hand-built dictionary is a minimal version of what a tokenizer's vocabulary-building (adapt) step automates later in the chapter.

concepts.name: Word-level tokenization with regex
concepts.definition: Splitting text into word and punctuation tokens with a regex such as [\w]+|[.,!?;].
concepts.intuition: Grab each run of letters as a word; grab each punctuation mark on its own; skip the spaces.
concepts.technical: re.findall scans left to right and returns every non-overlapping match. Each match is either a maximal run of \w characters or one character from [.,!?;]. Characters matching neither (spaces, apostrophes, hyphens, quotes) are discarded.
concepts.significance: Shorter sequences than character tokenization, with tokens that carry meaning.
concepts.example: split_words("The quick brown fox jumped over the dog.") -> ["The", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumped", "over", "the", "dog", "."]
concepts.misconception: It does not lowercase: "The" and "the" are different tokens unless the text is standardized first (p.410).

concepts.name: Indexing
concepts.definition: Mapping each token to a unique integer index.
concepts.intuition: Give every distinct token a ticket number.
concepts.technical: A function from tokens to integers in 0..V-1, applied element-wise to a token sequence. The integers have no numeric meaning; they are identifiers later turned into vectors (one-hot or embedding rows).
concepts.significance: The book calls it "by far the most common approach" to making tokens numeric, flexible and reversible.
concepts.misconception: Index 4 is not "twice" index 2; feeding raw indices into a dense layer as magnitudes would impose a false ordering.

concepts.name: Vocabulary
concepts.definition: A mapping from specific tokens occurring in the training data to integer indices.
concepts.intuition: A dictionary of only the words (or characters) you have actually seen, each with a number.
concepts.technical: Usually built by counting tokens in the training set, keeping the most frequent ones, and reserving indices for special tokens such as [UNK] (and, in Keras, a padding index). Its size V determines one-hot dimension and embedding-table rows.
concepts.significance: More robust than global character codes (ASCII/Unicode) and the only option for word tokens; it works for any token granularity.
concepts.misconception: A vocabulary is not the full language: it is limited to the training data, so unseen tokens need a fallback ([UNK], p.410).

concepts.name: Regex character classes and alternation
concepts.definition: [...] matches one listed character, \w matches a word character, + repeats one or more times, | chooses between alternatives.
concepts.intuition: Small building blocks combine into a tokenizer rule.
concepts.technical: [\w]+|[.,!?;] matches either a maximal run of word characters or one punctuation mark. Alternatives are tried left to right at each position.
concepts.significance: Changing the pattern changes the tokenizer without other code changes.
concepts.misconception: The book describes [\w]+ as matching "non-whitespace characters"; strictly it matches word characters, so apostrophes and hyphens are excluded.

parameters.name: r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]"
parameters.role: Tokenization rule: words or single punctuation marks.

pitfalls: Apostrophes, hyphens, quotes, colons and other symbols not in [.,!?;] are silently dropped: "isn't" -> ["isn", "t"], "state-of-the-art" -> four words.

code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written illustration (not from the book)
import re
split_words = lambda t: re.findall(r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]", t)
print(split_words("Isn't nature splendid??"))
# ['Isn', 't', 'nature', 'splendid', '?', '?']
print(split_words("México: 2024!"))
# ['México', '2024', '!']   (colon dropped; \w is Unicode-aware)

deeper.title: Tracing the word regex on "over the dog."
deeper.body:
Pattern: `[\w]+|[.,!?;]`

1. Position 0 `o`: `[\w]+` matches greedily `over`, which becomes a token.
2. Space: matches neither alternative and is skipped.
3. `the` becomes a token; the space is skipped.
4. `dog` matches `[\w]+`, stopping at `.` because `.` is not a word character.
5. `.`: the first alternative fails, the second `[.,!?;]` matches, giving token `.`.

Result: `["over", "the", "dog", "."]`.

deeper.title: Why not just use ord() codes?
deeper.body: If indices feed a one-hot encoding or an embedding table, the table needs one row per possible index. Using Unicode code points means up to 1,114,112 rows, while an English character vocabulary needs maybe 100 rows. For words there is no global code at all. A vocabulary built from training data keeps V small and only covers tokens that actually occur. (Numbers are an illustration, not from the book.)

deeper.title: A vocabulary is like a cloakroom ticket system
deeper.body: Each distinct coat (token) gets a numbered ticket (index) the first time it is seen. The number tells you nothing about the coat; it only lets you get the same coat back (reversibility). A coat with no ticket goes to the "unknown" rack, ticket 0.

misconceptions.claim: [\w]+ matches any run of non-whitespace characters.
misconceptions.correction: It matches word characters only (letters, digits, underscore). Non-whitespace is \S; with \w, apostrophes and hyphens are excluded, so "isn't" splits into "isn" and "t".

misconceptions.claim: Token indices are meaningful numbers the model can compare by size.
misconceptions.correction: They are arbitrary identifiers; the model later maps them into a latent space (e.g. embeddings), as the page notes.

misconceptions.claim: ASCII codes are a good universal index for characters.
misconceptions.correction: They scale poorly to other languages; Unicode has over a million characters. A vocabulary built from the training data is more robust.

takeaways: Character splitting keeps every character, spaces included, as a token.
The regex [\w]+|[.,!?;] splits text into words and single punctuation marks, dropping whitespace.
Indexing, which maps each token to a unique integer, is the most common way to make tokens numeric; it is flexible and reversible.
How indices become vectors (the latent space) is a separate, later choice.
ASCII/Unicode codes scale poorly; a vocabulary built from training data works for both characters and words.
The hand-built vocabulary reserves index 0 for [UNK].

questions.question: What does split_words("Wait, what?") return?
questions.explanation: [\w]+ grabs each word, [.,!?;] grabs "," and "?" as separate tokens, and the space is skipped. The first drops punctuation, the second glues punctuation to words (that would be whitespace splitting), and the fourth is character-level.

questions.question: Why do the authors prefer a vocabulary to ASCII lookups such as ord('A') -> 65?
questions.answer: ASCII/Unicode indexing scales poorly to other languages (Unicode has over a million characters), while a vocabulary maps only the tokens that occur in our data and works equally for words and characters.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph beginning "For character tokens...".

questions.question: What two properties of indexing does the page highlight?
questions.answer: It is flexible (it works with a wide range of modelling approaches) and reversible (indices can be mapped back to tokens).
questions.explanation: "This is a flexible and reversible representation of our tokenized input that can work with a wide range of modeling approaches."

questions.question: Which input would split_words handle in a way you might not want?
questions.explanation: The apostrophe is neither a word character nor in [.,!?;], so it is dropped and "isn't" becomes ["isn", "t"]. The others contain only word characters, spaces and listed punctuation, which split cleanly.

questions.question: The example sentence has 45 characters and split_words gives 10 tokens for it. If each token gets a one-hot vector, compare the vector dimension needed for raw Unicode code points with a word vocabulary of the 9 entries on pp.409-410.
questions.answer: Unicode code points would need about 1.1 million dimensions (0..1,114,111), while the vocabulary needs only 9 (indices 0-8).
questions.explanation: One-hot dimension equals the size of the index space. This is the scaling problem the page points to with "over a million characters in the Unicode specification."

questions.question: Explain in your own words the difference between splitting and indexing, and which one decides the latent space.
questions.answer: Splitting turns a string into string tokens; indexing maps tokens to integers. Neither decides the latent space; mapping indices to vectors is a later modelling choice.
questions.explanation: The page: "Later on, we can decide how to map from token indices into a latent space ingested by the model."
